section_summaries.epidemiology: Ascariasis is the most prevalent human helminth infection, affecting an estimated 819 million people worldwide, particularly in children under 10 years. Morbidity and transmission are related to worm burden, which is over-dispersed. Prevalence is highest in warm, humid equatorial regions, with approximately 72% of infections in Asia, 14% in sub-Saharan Africa, and 11% in Latin America and the Caribbean. Distribution is linked to land surface temperature and rainfall, as well as hygiene, sanitation, and socioeconomic status. A. lumbricoides has no significant animal reservoir, though A. suum can occasionally infect humans. Intensity of infection is not uniform, with a small proportion of the population harboring the majority of worms, concentrated in children. Infection is equally common in urban and rural settings.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Adult female Ascaris lumbricoides reside in the distal small intestine, producing up to 200,000 eggs daily. Infectious second-stage larvae, after ingestion or inhalation, hatch in the jejunum, penetrate the intestinal wall, and migrate via hepatic venules to the heart and pulmonary circulation. They break into alveolar spaces, undergo molts, and then ascend to the trachea to be swallowed and mature into adults in the intestine. Larval migration through the lungs can induce pulmonary hypersensitivity, presenting as asthma with eosinophilic inflammation and granulomatous reaction. The intestinal phase can lead to disturbances in nutrient absorption (lactose, nitrogen, vitamin A) and contribute to growth faltering. Heavy worm burdens can cause serious complications, most commonly terminal ileum obstruction in children under 10 years old. The life cycle from egg ingestion to egg production takes 10 to 12 weeks; adult worms live for approximately a year. The human immune response involves a strong localized T helper cell type 2 (Th2) response and immune hyporesponsiveness mediated by regulatory T cells and IL-10 production, which can influence allergic and autoimmune responses, and vaccine efficacy.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Most ascariasis infections have insidious effects on growth and development, including cognitive development. Heavy worm burdens, especially in young children, can lead to intestinal obstruction, most frequently reported as obstruction of the terminal ileum. Larval migration through the lungs can cause pulmonary hypersensitivity in sensitized hosts, leading to Löffler's syndrome with symptoms like fever, cough, wheezing, dyspnea, sputum production (sometimes bloody), chest pain, and cyanosis in severe cases. Chest film abnormalities may include nodular densities or diffuse interstitial patterns. The intestinal phase is generally asymptomatic, but moderate to heavy infections can cause appetite loss and malabsorption of nutrients. Migrating adult worms can lead to serious complications such as vomiting or passing worms per rectum, and entering ducts or diverticula, causing obstruction (e.g., common bile duct obstruction leading to biliary colic or cholangitis, pancreatic duct obstruction leading to pancreatitis) or perforation. Appendicitis can also be triggered by Ascaris obstruction of the appendix. Rarely, volvulus or ileocecal intussusception can occur.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis is typically made by direct fecal smear in saline, identifying characteristic A. lumbricoides eggs (55-75 µm by 35-50 µm) in direct or concentrated stool specimens. Unfertilized and decorticate eggs can be more challenging to identify due to atypical size or lack of outer mamillated covering, respectively, though the thick hyaline shell is characteristic. PCR-based diagnosis offers higher sensitivity. Infections by male-only worms do not produce eggs. Barium studies can visualize worms in the GI tract as thin, curved linear densities. Duodenoscopy with retrograde cholangiopancreatography and ultrasonography are useful for diagnosing biliary ascariasis and pancreatitis, respectively, and can aid in worm removal.
section_summaries.treatment: Ascariasis is effectively treated with several well-tolerated drugs, achieving cure rates over 90%. Mebendazole (100 mg twice daily for 3 days or 500 mg single dose) and albendazole (400 mg single dose) are highly effective and often donated for school-based deworming programs. Benzimidazoles should be avoided during the first trimester of pregnancy or in infants under 12 months, though children aged 12-24 months can receive supervised treatment. Levamisole (2.5 mg/kg) is similarly efficacious but withdrawn from some markets due to agranulocytosis. Oxantel pamoate with pyrantel is well-tolerated and effective but limited geographically. Side effects are transient and related to the GI tract. Intestinal obstruction may require surgery, but clinically stable and hydrated patients can often be managed conservatively with nasogastric suction, intravenous hydration, and anti-spasmodics, followed by anti-helminthics after obstruction subsides to avoid complete paralysis of worms. Obstruction of bile or pancreatic ducts may necessitate endoscopic or surgical intervention.
section_summaries.prevention: Re-infection is common due to egg viability in the environment, emphasizing the need for improved sanitation and hygiene. Chemotherapy delivered through school-based programs targeting school-age children is a feasible and effective approach to worm control, reducing morbidity and improving growth. Repeated chemotherapy in this age group also reduces community transmission, worm burden, and morbidity.
